cands.bio: U.S. Representative for California's 51st District, previously the 53rd, since January 2021. Earlier worked at the UN and UNICEF, as a State Department contractor and on Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign. She also led the nonprofits Project Connect and San Diego for Every Child.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed on Ballotpedia include the Democratic Party of California, California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), California Teachers Association, California Environmental Voters and Equality California.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions or actions on data centers, homestead property tax relief, limits on investor or foreign buyers of homes and land, or police pay and pensions. The policy statements we could read come from her 2020 campaign website, so they may not reflect her current positions. She did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in 2020, 2022, 2024 or 2026. We found no documented controversies in the pages we read.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: Six years in the U.S. House (since 2021) on the Armed Services and Foreign Affairs committees. Before that, policy work at the UN, UNICEF and as a State Department contractor, a policy advisor role on Clinton's 2016 campaign, and CEO of the nonprofit Project Connect.
qual.why: Holding federal legislative office gives her direct experience in lawmaking, oversight and constituent service, which puts her in the high band. Her earlier policy and international work adds to that.

second-amendment.evidence: On her 2020 campaign website she said she supports a federal assault weapons ban, federal red flag laws, universal background checks, federal gun licensing and background checks on ammunition sales.

pro-life.evidence: Authored the My Body, My Data Act in 2022 to limit the collection of personal reproductive health data, and reintroduced it in 2023 and 2025; Wikipedia lists it under her abortion-rights work.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: On her 2020 campaign website she said, 'I oppose vouchers because they divert resources from our public school system.'

clean-money.evidence: On her 2020 campaign website she said she signed the No Fossil Fuel Money Pledge and would not accept money from oil, gas and coal executives, lobbyists or corporate PACs.

cands.name: Ricardo Cabrera
cands.bio: Republican candidate for California's 51st Congressional District in 2026. Describes himself as a San Diegan, small business owner and cybersecurity professional. Ballotpedia lists his profession as chief executive officer. He has held no elected office.
cands.gaps: We couldn't find where Cabrera was born or raised, or when he moved to California. We found no details on his business or cybersecurity employers, or on what his CEO role involved. He has no record in office. We found nothing on his stances on data centers, development and land use, immigration and H-1B, guns, abortion, policing or school choice. His only housing and tax statements are general remarks about affordability and taxes. We found no documented controversies or foreign ties.
